title.en: T'ien Tzŭ Fang's Tutor: In Appearance a Man, in Reality God (Zhuangzi)
title.zh: 田子方之師東郭順子（莊子）

region.en: The Wei court (Anyang region, Henan, China)

texts.period: Zhuangzi ch. 21, c. 4th-3rd c. BCE (trans. Giles, 1889)

source.work: Chuang Tzu: Mystic, Moralist, and Social Reformer, trans. Herbert A. Giles, ch. 21

summary.en: T'ien Tzŭ Fang praises a mere neighbour, Ch'i Kung, but not his own tutor Tung Kuo Shun Tzŭ — because the tutor is perfect: in appearance a man, in reality God; unconditioned himself, he falls in with the conditioned. Prince Wên remains absorbed in silence for the rest of the day: how far beyond us is the man of perfect virtue!
summary.zh: 田子方侍坐於魏文侯，稱谿工——吾師東郭順子：其為人也真，人貌而天虛，緣而葆真，清而容物。文侯曰：吾於聖賢之道，不以自望矣。

sensitivity.note: Canonical text of the Taoist canon (Nanhua zhenjing). Included as a comparative text — a scholarly framing, not a claim about religious truth.

passages.text: "Then how is it you do not praise him?" asked the Prince. "He is perfect," replied Tzŭ Fang. "In appearance, a man; in reality, God. Unconditioned himself, he falls in with the conditioned, to his own greater glory. Pure himself, he can still tolerate others. If men are without TAO, by a mere look he calls them to a sense of error, and causes their intentions to melt away. How could I praise him?"

Thereupon Tzŭ Fang took his leave, and the Prince remained for the rest of the day absorbed in silence. At length he called an officer in waiting and said, "How far beyond us is the man of perfect virtue! Hitherto I have regarded the discussion of holiness and wisdom, and the practice of charity and duty to one's neighbour, as the utmost point attainable. But now that I have heard of Tzŭ Fang's tutor, my body is relaxed and desires not movement, my mouth is closed and desires not speech. All I have learnt, verily it is mere undergrowth. And the kingdom of Wei is my bane."

title.en: The Visitor Who Was Now Dragon, Now Tiger (Zhuangzi)

region.en: Lu, on the way to Ch'i (Qufu, Shandong, China)

texts.period: Zhuangzi ch. 21, c. 4th-3rd c. BCE (trans. Giles, 1889)

source.work: Chuang Tzu: Mystic, Moralist, and Social Reformer, trans. Herbert A. Giles, ch. 21

summary.en: Wên Po Hsüeh Tzŭ, breaking his journey in Lu, receives a stranger twice and sighs after each visit: the man came and went as per compasses and square, his demeanour was now that of the dragon, now that of the tiger; he criticised me as though he had been my son, admonished me as though he had been my father. Confucius, meeting Wên Po Hsüeh Tzŭ, says nothing — with such men as these, you have only to look, and TAO abides.
summary.zh: 溫伯雪子適齊，舍於魯；見客而嘆——其為人也，動容其色，觸目皆真。仲尼見之而不言；曰：若夫人者，目擊而道存矣，亦不可以容聲矣。

sensitivity.note: Canonical text of the Taoist canon (Nanhua zhenjing). Included as a comparative text — a scholarly framing, not a claim about religious truth.

passages.text: "I have already told you," replied Wên Po Hsüeh Tzŭ, "that the people of the Middle Kingdom are experts in ceremonies and obligations but wanting in knowledge of the human heart. The man who visited me came in and went out as per compasses and square. His demeanour was now that of the dragon, now that of the tiger. He criticised me as though he had been my son. He admonished me as though he had been my father. Therefore I gave vent to sighs."

When Confucius saw Wên Po Hsüeh Tzŭ, the former did not utter a word. Whereupon Tzŭ Lu said, "Master, you have long wished to see Wên Po Hsüeh Tzŭ. How is it that when you do see him you do not speak?" "With such men as these," replied Confucius, "you have only to look, and TAO abides. There is no room for speech."

region.en: The court of Lu (Qufu, Shandong, China)

texts.period: Zhuangzi ch. 21, c. 4th-3rd c. BCE (trans. Giles, 1889)

source.work: Chuang Tzu: Mystic, Moralist, and Social Reformer, trans. Herbert A. Giles, ch. 21

summary.en: Yen Yüan follows Confucius at a walk, a trot, and a gallop — but when his master dashes beyond the bounds of mortality he can only stand staring behind. Confucius answers that there is no sorrow to be compared with the death of the mind, and that although his old self is constantly passing away, there remains that which does not pass away.
summary.zh: 顏淵問於仲尼：夫子步亦步，夫子趨亦趨，夫子馳亦馳——夫子奔逸絕塵，而回瞠若乎後矣！仲尼曰：哀莫大於心死，而人死亦次之。

sensitivity.note: Canonical text of the Taoist canon (Nanhua zhenjing). Included as a comparative text — a scholarly framing, not a claim about religious truth.

passages.text: Yen Yüan asked Confucius, saying, "Master, when you go at a walk, I go at a walk. When you trot, I trot. When you gallop, I gallop. But when you dash beyond the bounds of mortality, I can only stand staring behind. How is this?" "What is there to prevent you from finding out?" replied Confucius. "There is no sorrow to be compared with the death of the mind. The death of the body is of but secondary importance.

"Now you fix your attention upon something in me which, while you look, has already passed away. Yet you seek for it as though it must be still there,--like one who seeks for a horse in a market-place. What I admire in you is transitory. Nevertheless, why should you grieve? Although my old self is constantly passing away, there remains that which does not pass away."

title.en: Lao Tzŭ Wandering in the Unborn (Zhuangzi)
title.zh: 老聃遊心於物之初（莊子）

region.en: Lao Tzŭ's chamber (symbolic pin: Ku county, Bozhou, Anhui, China)
region.zh: 老聃之室（象徵定位：安徽亳州苦縣）

texts.period: Zhuangzi ch. 21, c. 4th-3rd c. BCE (trans. Giles, 1889)

source.work: Chuang Tzu: Mystic, Moralist, and Social Reformer, trans. Herbert A. Giles, ch. 21

summary.en: Confucius finds Lao Tzŭ, freshly washed and hair hanging to dry, looking like a lifeless body — I was wandering in the unborn, says Lao Tzŭ. The perfect Negative is majestically passive, the perfect Positive powerfully active; their interaction results in the harmony by which all things are produced. There may be a First Cause, but we never see his form. Heaven is naturally high, the earth naturally solid — do they cultivate these attributes?
summary.zh: 孔子見老聃；老聃新沐，方將被髮而乾，慹然似非人。曰：吾遊心於物之初——至陰肅肅，至陽赫赫；交通成和而物生焉。

sensitivity.note: Canonical text of the Taoist canon (Nanhua zhenjing); the yin-yang cosmogony in Laozi's mouth. Included as a comparative text.

passages.text: Confucius went to see Lao Tzŭ. The latter had just washed his head, and his hair was hanging down his back to dry. He looked like a lifeless body; so Confucius waited awhile, but at length approached and said, "Do my eyes deceive me, or is this really so? Your frame, Sir, seems like dry wood, as if it had been left without that which informs it with the life of man." "I was wandering," replied Lao Tzŭ, "in the unborn."

"The perfect Negative principle is majestically passive. The perfect Positive principle is powerfully active. Passivity emanates from heaven above; activity proceeds from earth beneath. The interaction of the two results in that harmony by which all things are produced. There may be a First Cause, but we never see his form. His report fills space. There is darkness and light. Days come and months go. Work is being constantly performed, yet we never witness the performance. Life must bring us from somewhere, and death must carry us back. Beginning and end follow ceaselessly one upon the other, and we cannot say when the series will be exhausted. If this is not the work of a First Cause, what is it?"

"Not so," answered Lao Tzŭ. "The fluidity of water is not the result of any effort on the part of the water, but is its natural property. And the virtue of the perfect man is such that even without cultivation there is nothing which can withdraw from his sway. Heaven is naturally high, the earth is naturally solid, the sun and moon are naturally bright. Do they cultivate these attributes?"

title.en: The One Scholar Robed in Lu (Zhuangzi)
title.zh: 魯少儒：哀公五日之令（莊子）

region.en: The court of Duke Ai of Lu (Qufu, Shandong, China)
region.zh: 魯哀公之廷（今山東曲阜）

texts.period: Zhuangzi ch. 21, c. 4th-3rd c. BCE (trans. Giles, 1889)

source.work: Chuang Tzu: Mystic, Moralist, and Social Reformer, trans. Herbert A. Giles, ch. 21

summary.en: Duke Ai boasts that Lu is full of scholars in scholars' robes. Chuang Tzŭ proposes death for any who wear the robes without having the TAO; after five days of the mandate not a single man in Lu dares to don scholars' robes — except one old man who stands at the Duke's gate, whom entangling questions on politics fail to entangle. If there is only one scholar in Lu, surely that is not many.
summary.zh: 莊子見魯哀公——儒者圓冠圜履者：知天時；方屨者：知地形；緩佩玦者：事至而斷。無此而服此者，其罪死——於是乎魯國無敢儒服者。

sensitivity.note: Canonical text of the Taoist canon (Nanhua zhenjing). Included as a comparative text — a scholarly framing, not a claim about religious truth.

passages.text: When Chuang Tzŭ was at an interview with Duke Ai of Lu, the latter said, "We have many scholars, Sir, in Lu, but few of your school." "In Lu," replied Chuang Tzŭ, "there are but few scholars." "Look at the number who wear scholars' robes," said the Duke. "How can you say they are few?" "Scholars who wear round hats," answered Chuang Tzŭ, "know the seasons of Heaven. Scholars who wear square shoes know the shape of Earth. And scholars who loosely gird themselves are ready to decide whatever questions may arise. But scholars who have TAO do not necessarily wear robes; neither does the wearing of robes necessarily mean that a scholar has TAO. If your Highness does not think so, why not issue an order through the Middle Kingdom, making death the punishment for all who wear the robes without having the TAO?"

Thereupon Duke Ai circulated this mandate for five days, the result being that not a single man in Lu dared to don scholars' robes,--with the exception of one old man who, thus arrayed, took his stand at the Duke's gate. The Duke summoned him to the presence, and asked him many questions on politics, trying to entangle him, but in vain. Then Chuang Tzŭ said, "If there is only one scholar in Lu, surely that is not many."

title.en: The Fisherman of Tsang and Wên Wang's Dream (Zhuangzi)

region.en: The river at Tsang, land of Chou (Baoji region, Shaanxi, China)
region.zh: 臧地之濱（象徵定位：陝西寶雞）

texts.period: Zhuangzi ch. 21, c. 4th-3rd c. BCE (trans. Giles, 1889)

source.work: Chuang Tzu: Mystic, Moralist, and Social Reformer, trans. Herbert A. Giles, ch. 21

summary.en: On a tour of inspection in Tsang, Wên Wang sees an old man fishing not to catch fish but to amuse himself. Wishing to employ him yet fearing the ministers' objections, Wên Wang tells his court a dream: a sage of black colour riding a parti-coloured horse instructed him to place the administration in the old man's hands. After three years, all dangerous organisations are broken up — and when asked if such government can extend over the empire, the old man takes leave and by evening has disappeared, never to be heard of again.
summary.zh: 文王觀於臧，見一丈夫釣，而其釣莫釣。乃託夢：臧地之老人可授政——三年，將以政東旋；問：可達於天下乎？釣者不言而別，終身無聞。

sensitivity.note: Canonical text of the Taoist canon (Nanhua zhenjing); the dream-sanctioned ministry is a kingmaking topos. Included as a comparative text.

passages.text: When Wên Wang was on a tour of inspection in Tsang, he saw an old man fishing. But his fishing was not real fishing, for he did not fish to catch fish, but to amuse himself. So Wên Wang wished to employ him in the administration of government, but feared lest his own ministers, uncles, and brothers, might object. Accordingly, that very morning he informed his ministers, saying, "I once dreamt that a Sage of a black colour and with a large beard, riding upon a parti-coloured horse with red stockings on one side, appeared and instructed me to place the administration in the hands of the old gentleman of Tsang, promising that the people would benefit greatly thereby."

The ministers at once said, "It is a command from your Highness' father." "I think so," answered Wên Wang. "But let us try by divination." "It is a command from your Highness' late father," said the ministers, "and may not be disobeyed. What need for divination?" So the old man of Tsang was received and entrusted with the administration. He altered none of the existing statutes. He issued no unjust regulations. And when, after three years, Wên Wang made another inspection, he found all dangerous organisations broken up, the officials doing their duty as a matter of course, while the use of measures of grain was unknown within the four boundaries of the State.

So Wên Wang appointed the old man Grand Tutor; and then, standing with his face to the north, asked him, saying, "Can such government be extended over the empire?" The old man of Tsang was silent and made no reply. He then abruptly took leave, and by the evening of that same day had disappeared, never to be heard of again. Yen Yüan said to Confucius, "If Wên Wang was unable to do this of himself, how was he able to do it by a dream?" "Silence!" cried Confucius: "It is not for you to criticise Wên Wang who succeeded in fulfilling his mission. The dream was merely to satisfy the vulgar mind."

title.en: Shooting from a Precipice a Thousand Feet High (Zhuangzi)
title.zh: 列禦寇之射與伯昏無人之懸崖（莊子）

region.en: The thousand-foot precipice (symbolic pin: Huashan, Shaanxi, China)
region.zh: 千仞之崖（象徵定位：陝西華山）

texts.period: Zhuangzi ch. 21, c. 4th-3rd c. BCE (trans. Giles, 1889)

source.work: Chuang Tzu: Mystic, Moralist, and Social Reformer, trans. Herbert A. Giles, ch. 21

summary.en: Lieh Yü K'ou demonstrates archery with a cup of water on his elbow, arrow after arrow, standing like a statue. Po Hun Wu Jên leads him up a mountain to the edge of a precipice a thousand feet high and beckons him on; Lieh Tzŭ falls prostrate with the sweat pouring down to his heels. The perfect man soars up to the blue sky or dives down to the yellow springs without change of countenance.
summary.zh: 列禦寇為伯昏無人射，引之盈貫，措杯水其肘上——登高山，履危石，臨百仞之淵。吾嘗見其瞋恙，而神慚焉。

sensitivity.note: Canonical text of the Taoist canon (Nanhua zhenjing). Included as a comparative text — a scholarly framing, not a claim about religious truth.

passages.text: Lieh Yü K'ou instructed Po Hun Wu Jên in archery. Drawing the bow to its full, he placed a cup of water on his elbow and began to let fly. Hardly was one arrow out of sight ere another was on the string, the archer standing all the time like a statue. "But this is shooting under ordinary conditions," cried Po Hun Wu Jên; "it is not shooting under extraordinary conditions. Now I will ascend a high mountain with you, and stand on the edge of a precipice a thousand feet in height, and see how you can shoot then."

Thereupon Wu Jên went with Lieh Tzŭ up a high mountain, and stood on the edge of a precipice a thousand feet in height, approaching it backwards until one-fifth of his feet overhung the chasm, when he beckoned to Lieh Tzŭ to come on. But the latter had fallen prostrate on the ground, with the sweat pouring down to his heels. "The perfect man," said Wu Jên, "soars up to the blue sky, or dives down to the yellow springs, or flies to some extreme point of the compass, without change of countenance. But you are terrified, and your eyes are dazed. Your internal economy is defective."

title.en: Sun Shu Ao Thrice Called and Thrice Dismissed (Zhuangzi)
title.zh: 孫叔敖三為令尹而不榮（莊子）

texts.period: Zhuangzi ch. 21, c. 4th-3rd c. BCE (trans. Giles, 1889)

source.work: Chuang Tzu: Mystic, Moralist, and Social Reformer, trans. Herbert A. Giles, ch. 21

summary.en: Chien Wu marvels that Sun Shu Ao was three times called to office without elation and three times dismissed without chagrin, his breathing perfectly regular. The souls of such men pierced through huge mountains as though they had been nothing, descended into the abyss without getting wet — they filled the whole universe; and the more they gave to others, the more they had themselves.
summary.zh: 肩吾問於孫叔敖曰：子三為令尹而不榮華，三去之而無憂色。孫叔敖曰：吾何以過人哉？吾以其來不可卻也，其去不可止也。

sensitivity.note: Canonical text of the Taoist canon (Nanhua zhenjing). Included as a comparative text — a scholarly framing, not a claim about religious truth.

passages.text: Chien Wu said to Sun Shu Ao, "Sir, you have been three times called to office without showing any elation, and you have been three times dismissed without displaying any chagrin. At first, I doubted you; but now I notice that your breathing is perfectly regular. How do you manage thus to control your emotions?" "I am no better than other people," replied Sun Shu Ao. "I regard office when it comes as something which may not be declined; when it goes, as something which cannot be kept. To me both the getting and losing are outside my own self; and therefore I feel no chagrin."

When Confucius heard this, he said, "The perfect Sages of old!--cunning men could not defeat them; beautiful women could not seduce them; robbers could not steal from them; Fu Hsi and the Yellow Emperor could not make friends of them. Life and death are great; yet these gave them no pang. How much less then rank and power! "The souls of such men pierced through huge mountains as though they had been nothing; descended into the abyss without getting wet; occupied lowly stations without chagrin. They filled the whole universe; and the more they gave to others, the more they had themselves."
